extracted.intended_audience: trademark practitioners, USPTO examining attorneys, and parties/applicants involved in TTAB proceedings and trademark prosecution
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on what evidence is acceptable, how it must be submitted, and procedural rules for judicial notice, use of Internet and third-party materials, applicant materials, and Board remands in ex parte trademark examination and TTAB appeals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representative sampling of media/search results
rubrics_metrics.description: When submitting a subset of numerous search results or press stories, the submitting party should indicate whether the submitted excerpts are a representative sample; mere saying they are a 'sample' is not the same as demonstrating they are 'representative'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If many items are retrieved, submitting only a few excerpts without indicating representativeness may lead the Board to conclude the unsubmitted items do not support the submitting party’s position. Examining attorneys/applicants should avoid submitting only a small, unexplained subset of a much larger retrieval; if additional stories exist that support the position, a larger number should be submitted and representativeness addressed. See cases criticizing submission of only select excerpts (e.g., In re Trans Continental Records; In re Homes & Land; In re Monotype).

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive, duplicative, or irrelevant Internet material
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties should submit only relevant Internet materials and avoid creating an unduly large or duplicative record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board discourages submissions that are unnecessarily cumulative or not probative. Large-volume submissions (e.g., hundreds of pages) that are duplicative, reference different terms, or concern unrelated goods/services may be criticized and largely unhelpful. When many web pages are submitted, parties should highlight in briefs the most probative pieces of evidence so the Board can consider them in particular (see In re Max Capital Group Ltd.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include full URL and download date for web evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Internet/website printouts are acceptable evidence, but it is preferable to identify web pages by full address (URL) and the date downloaded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The download date may be shown on the page itself or provided separately in an Office action or response. These details help verify the content because website contents can change. Website evidence may show public exposure, translations, product/service information, customers, and channels of trade; probative value depends on the case facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limited probative value of search engine result summaries and hit counts
rubrics_metrics.description: Search engine result summaries and raw hit counts are of limited or no probative value for showing how a term is used or the relevance/extent of use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search summaries may lack context (headings, links, or surrounding text), and large numbers of hits do not corroborate that many relevant references exist. Google/Yahoo hit lists or truncated excerpts often provide insufficient context to determine nature of use; exceptions exist where the summary contains enough context to understand usage (see In re Hotels.com).

rubrics_metrics.name: Online dictionary and Wikipedia evidence — limits and best practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Definitions from online resources are acceptable if they are readily verifiable, especially if they are electronic equivalents of print references; Wikipedia may be considered but is best corroborated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will generally not take judicial notice of online-only references unless they are electronic equivalents of print references or have regular fixed editions. Online-only dictionary definitions should be submitted prior to appeal to allow rebuttal. The Board will consider Wikipedia evidence if the nonoffering party has the opportunity to rebut; better practice is to corroborate Wikipedia content with reliable sources and cite Wikipedia’s sources where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial notice — permissible reference works and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may take judicial notice of dictionary definitions (including technical/translation/slang), encyclopedia entries, standard reference works, and commonly known facts, subject to limits regarding online-only sources and foreign usage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board will not generally take judicial notice of definitions or entries found only in online reference works unless they are electronic equivalents of print works or have fixed editions. The Board will not take judicial notice of terms based on English spoken in another country, and will not rely solely on a web address/link to consider site content. See TBMP § 704.12 for full discussion and many cited cases where judicial notice was or was not taken.

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-party registrations — record submission and probative value
rubrics_metrics.description: Third-party registrations should be made of record during prosecution/examination by submitting copies of the registrations or Office records; mere listings or private search reports are generally insufficient and have limited probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under 37 C.F.R. § 2.142(d) the record must be complete prior to appeal; the Board ordinarily will not take judicial notice of third-party registrations presented for the first time during appeal. If an applicant only provides lists of registration numbers/marks, those lists have limited probative value. Expired or cancelled registrations generally only evidence that registrations issued; the Board may decline to consider them. Third-party applications have no probative value beyond showing an application was filed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver and stipulation exceptions for third-party listings
rubrics_metrics.description: If an applicant submits a listing of third-party registrations during prosecution and the examining attorney fails to advise it is insufficient (when there's time to cure), the examining attorney may be deemed to have waived objection; if the examining attorney discusses registrations without objecting, they may be treated as stipulated into the record.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an examining attorney treats a listing as of record or fails to object at a time when the applicant could fix the deficiency, the Board has considered such listings for whatever probative value they may have. However, this does not authorize submission of full registrations for the first time on appeal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improper or untimely listings will not be considered
rubrics_metrics.description: Listings of third-party registrations submitted at a point when the submitting party cannot correct the format or when the examining attorney objects and did not treat them as of record will not be considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include lists submitted with a request for reconsideration when the applicant no longer can add to the record, or lists from unidentified sources submitted with objections. Timeliness and the opportunity to cure evidentiary defects are critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant’s own materials and submissions
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s materials (websites, advertisements, specimens) may be considered even if the application is based on intent-to-use or later changed to intent-to-use; applicant-submitted expert reports and surveys are considered for their probative value.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examining attorneys may introduce applicant literature showing descriptiveness. Specimens submitted under one filing basis remain of record if the basis changes. Expert reports and surveys are weighed according to their probative value in the case.

rubrics_metrics.name: Board remand procedure and timing (sua sponte or on issue raised)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the Board identifies an issue not previously raised that may render the mark unregistrable, it may suspend appeal and remand the application to the examining attorney for further examination, generally to be completed within 30 days.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no new ground results, the examiner returns the application with a written statement and the Board resumes the appeal. If further examination yields an additional ground and it is made final, the appellant gets 60 days to file a supplemental brief limited to that ground (failure may lead to dismissal). The examiner must file a written answering brief within 60 days of the appellant's supplemental brief, and the appellant may reply within 20 days. Oral hearing procedures depend on whether an oral hearing was previously requested or held; an appellant may request one within 10 days after the due date for reply brief on the additional ground if not previously requested. The Board will not remand to consider a requirement/ground that the examining attorney previously raised and then withdrew; remands may also be for clarification when parties appear to be arguing different grounds.
